title: High preoperative CONUT score is associated with treatment failure and mortality after surgery for acute periprosthetic joint infection: a single-centre retrospective cohort study.
authors: Otero-Naveiro V, Ayuso-García B, Pena-Paz S, Rión-Giraldo RA, García-Pais MJ, López-Pardo Pardo A
abstract:
1. J Bone Jt Infect. 2026 Oct 13;11(5):613-622. doi: 10.5194/jbji-11-613-2026. 
eCollection 2026.

High preoperative CONUT score is associated with treatment failure and mortality 
after surgery for acute periprosthetic joint infection: a single-centre 
retrospective cohort study.

Otero-Naveiro V(1), Ayuso-García B(2), Pena-Paz S(1), Rión-Giraldo RA(1), 
García-Pais MJ(2), López-Pardo Pardo A(1).



Introduction: Acute periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is associated with 
substantial morbidity and mortality. The controlling nutritional status (CONUT) 
score combines serum albumin, total lymphocyte count, and total cholesterol, and 
may reflect host vulnerability. This study evaluated whether preoperative CONUT 
is associated with failure and mortality after surgery for acute PJI. Methods: 
We performed a single-centre retrospective cohort study of patients surgically 
treated for acute postoperative or acute haematogenous hip or knee PJI between 1 
January 2013 and 30 November 2024. PJI was defined according to EBJIS criteria. 
CONUT was calculated from preoperative blood tests and dichotomised as low (  <  
5; normal to mild) or high (  ≥  5; moderate to severe). Outcomes were defined 
using an adapted MSIS-ORT classification as failure, total failure including 
death within 1 year, and overall mortality. Results: Of 169 screened patients, 
59 were excluded for missing CONUT data and 90 were included; 42/90 (46.7 %) had 
high CONUT. High CONUT was associated with higher failure (35.7 % vs. 10.4 %; p 
= 0.004 ), total failure (57.1 % vs. 12.5 %; p < 0.001 ), and overall mortality 
(61.9 % vs. 22.9 %; p < 0.001 ). Adjusted analyses confirmed independent 
associations with failure (odds ratio (OR) 4.24, 95 % confidence interval (CI) 
1.34-13.46; p = 0.014 ), total failure (OR 9.57, 95 % CI 2.91-31.50; p < 0.001 
), and overall mortality (hazard ratio (HR) 2.73, 95 % CI 1.29-5.74; p = 0.008 
). Conclusions: High preoperative CONUT was associated with failure, total 
failure, and overall mortality after surgery for acute PJI. It may support risk 
stratification but should not be viewed solely as a nutritional marker, as its 
components may reflect systemic inflammation, bacteraemia, and infection 
severity.

title: Low graft failure after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in professional soccer players: A retrospective cohort study of 232 knees from the SANTI Study Group.
authors: Santamaria F, Santos PM, Ayata M, Wehbe H, Sonnery-Cottet V, Campos JP, Corti J, Vieira TD, Sonnery-Cottet B
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 15. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70641.
Online  ahead of print.

Low graft failure after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in 
professional soccer players: A retrospective cohort study of 232 knees from the 
SANTI Study Group.

Santamaria F(1), Santos PM(1), Ayata M(1), Wehbe H(1), Sonnery-Cottet V(1), 
Campos JP(2), Corti J(1), Vieira TD(1), Sonnery-Cottet B(1).



PURPOSE: This study aimed to determine graft failure rates after primary 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) in professional soccer players 
and to evaluate factors associated with graft failure, including lateral 
extra-articular augmentation.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 232 primary ACLRs in 215 
professional soccer players: isolated ACLR (n = 31) and ACLR combined with a 
lateral extra-articular procedure (LEAP) (n = 201). The primary endpoint was 
graft failure, defined as symptomatic rupture confirmed clinically and by 
imaging or revision surgery. Time-to-event analyses accounted for variable 
follow-up. Contralateral ACL injury was recorded descriptively.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 100 months, 13 graft failures occurred (5.6%). 
Unadjusted failure rates were lower in ACLR + LEAP versus isolated ACLR (4.5% 
vs. 12.9%), but survival analysis showed no significant difference (hazard ratio 
[HR] 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49-9.87; p = 0.246). Multivariable Cox 
regression identified no independent predictors of graft failure. Mean time to 
graft failure was longer in the ACLR + LEAP group than in the isolated ACLR 
group (54.8 ± 52.0 vs. 36.6 ± 38.2 months). Reoperations occurred in 32 knees 
(17.7%), with rates of 15.2% in the ACLR + LEAP group and 30.0% in the isolated 
ACLR group (p = 0.0528). Increased preoperative laxity (≥7 mm; HR 2.72; 95% CI 
1.23-6.17; p = 0.014) and bone-patellar tendon-bone graft use (HR 3.14; 95% CI 
1.26-7.20; p = 0.037) were independent risk factors for reoperation. 
Contralateral ACL injury occurred in 27.1% of knees, more frequently in female 
athletes (48.7% vs. 22.8%). Among patients who experienced graft failure, 53.8% 
also had a contralateral ACL injury.
CONCLUSION: Primary ACL reconstruction in professional soccer players was 
associated with durable long-term graft survival. Although ACLR combined with an 
LEAP was associated with fewer graft failures than isolated ACLR, an independent 
protective effect was not confirmed. The high rate of contralateral ACL injury 
highlights the multifactorial nature of reinjury risk in this elite population.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

DOI: 10.1002/ksa.70641
PMID: 42879166
ai_summary: In professional soccer players, ACL reconstruction shows excellent long-term durability, with high rates of contralateral injury regardless of whether a lateral extra-articular procedure was performed.

title: Sex-related differences after ACL reconstruction differ between early functional recovery and 5-year outcomes.
authors: Marty-Diloy T, Graveleau N, Bouguennec N
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 15. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70651.
Online  ahead of print.

Sex-related differences after ACL reconstruction differ between early functional 
recovery and 5-year outcomes.

Marty-Diloy T(1), Graveleau N(1), Bouguennec N(1).



PURPOSE: To compare early functional recovery and 5-year clinical, sports and 
psychological outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) 
according to sex.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who 
underwent primary ACLR between January 2017 and December 2019, with standardized 
6-month functional and psychological assessment and available 5-year follow-up. 
Patients were analyzed according to sex. Baseline characteristics, 6-month 
quadriceps strength and hop-test performance, and 5-year patient-reported and 
sports outcomes were compared between groups. The primary outcome was recovery 
of preinjury activity level at 5 years, defined as a post-operative Tegner score 
greater than or equal to the preoperative Tegner score. Multivariable logistic 
regression was used to identify factors independently associated with the 
primary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 479 patients were included, comprising 173 women (36.1%) and 
306 men (63.9%). At 6 months, men demonstrated higher quadriceps limb symmetry 
and lower hop-test deficits than women, whereas anterior cruciate ligament 
return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) did not differ significantly between 
groups. At 5 years, overall return-to-sport rates were similar between sexes 
(187 [61.2%] men vs. 103 [59.5%] women, p = 0.85), but men had higher 
post-operative Tegner (6 [5-7] vs. 5 [4-7], p < 0.001), IKDC (82.5 [75.7-87.3] 
vs. 79.5 [72.8-86.3], p = 0.02) and ACL-RSI scores (77.5 [55.8-92.5] vs. 69.2 
[53.3-85.8], p = 0.02) and were more likely to recover their preinjury activity 
level (137 [45.1%] vs. 48 [28.1%], p < 0.001). In the baseline-adjusted 
multivariable model, male sex was independently associated with recovery of 
preinjury activity level (odds ratio [OR] = 2.16, 95% confidence interval 
[CI] = 1.40-3.39; p < 0.001). This association persisted after inclusion of 
6-month recovery variables (OR = 1.93, 95% CI = 1.20-3.15; p = 0.007), while 
lower single-hop deficit was also independently associated with the outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Men and women did not demonstrate the same recovery profile after 
ACLR. Early differences were mainly functional, whereas 5-year differences 
involved recovery of preinjury activity level, subjective knee function and 
psychological readiness, despite similar overall return-to-sport rates. These 
findings suggest that return to sport should not be interpreted as equivalent 
recovery quality after ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

© 2026 European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy.

DOI: 10.1002/ksa.70651
PMID: 42879163
ai_summary: While men and women return to sports at similar rates after ACL surgery, men report higher long-term knee function and psychological readiness, suggesting sex-specific recovery milestones are needed.

title: Changes in Coronal and Sagittal Plane Alignment After Transphyseal ACL Reconstruction Performed Within Two Years of Skeletal Maturity: Results From the PLUTO Study Group.
authors: Bram JT, Saville GH, Whalen MM, Farah S, Sugimoto D, Green DW, PLUTO Study Group, Ganley TJ, Lawrence JTR, Perkins CA, Busch MT, Pennock AT, Chambers HG, Edmonds EW, Cordasco FA, Anderson CN, Heyworth BE, Matava MJ, Micheli LJ, Milewski MD, Nepple J, Parikh SN, Saluan PM, Shea KG, Wall EJ, Willimon SC, Kocher MS, Fabricant PD
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 15:3635465261492231. doi: 10.1177/03635465261492231.
 Online ahead of print.

Changes in Coronal and Sagittal Plane Alignment After Transphyseal ACL 
Reconstruction Performed Within Two Years of Skeletal Maturity: Results From the 
PLUTO Study Group.

Bram JT(1)(2), Saville GH(3)(2), Whalen MM(3)(2), Farah S(3)(2), Sugimoto 
D(3)(2), Green DW(1)(2); PLUTO Study Group(2); Ganley TJ(4)(2), Lawrence 
JTR(4)(2), Perkins CA(5)(2), Busch MT(5)(2), Pennock AT(6)(2), Chambers 
HG(6)(2), Edmonds EW(6)(2), Cordasco FA(1)(2), Anderson CN(7)(2), Heyworth 
BE(3)(2), Matava MJ(8)(2), Micheli LJ(3)(2), Milewski MD(3)(2), Nepple J(8)(2), 
Parikh SN(9)(2), Saluan PM(10)(2), Shea KG(11)(2), Wall EJ(9)(2), Willimon 
SC(5)(2), Kocher MS(3)(2), Fabricant PD(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: For patients with open physes approaching skeletal maturity, 
transphyseal anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) with soft tissue 
autograft and metaphyseal fixation is often preferred. Although iatrogenic 
physeal injury is rare, growth disturbances have been reported. This study 
sought to evaluate postoperative changes in lower extremity alignment 1 year 
after transphyseal ACLR in skeletally immature patients within 2 years of 
skeletal maturity.
HYPOTHESIS: Transphyseal ACLR would not result in clinically significant changes 
in alignment.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: This was a prospective multicenter study of skeletally immature 
patients with ≤2 years of remaining growth who underwent primary transphyseal 
soft tissue autograft ACLR. The change in the difference in alignment parameters 
between involved and uninvolved extremities from preoperative assessment to 1 
year postoperative was calculated (difference of differences = Δ2) to account 
for naturally occurring alignment changes during growth. Radiographic 
measurements included mechanical axis deviation (MAD), anatomic lateral distal 
femoral angle (aLDFA), mechanical medial proximal tibial angle (mMPTA), 
posterior tibial slope (PTS), and leg length discrepancy (LLD).
RESULTS: A total of 91 patients (48 males) merited inclusion with a median 
skeletal age of 14.0 years. Reconstructions were performed with hamstring (46%) 
or quadriceps (54%) autograft. The cohort-wide median Δ2 values for MAD (2.9 
mm), aLDFA (-1°), mMPTA (0°), and LLD (0.1 cm) were small. However, 28% of 
patients demonstrated a ≥10-mm Δ2 in MAD (73% into valgus), and Δ2 for aLDFA and 
mMPTA was ≥5° in 17% (73% into valgus) and 16% (43% into varus) of patients, 
respectively. One patient (1%) subsequently was recommended for intervention for 
growth disturbance at latest follow-up.
CONCLUSION: This study of skeletally immature individuals with ≤22 years of 
growth remaining who underwent transphyseal ACLR with soft tissue autograft and 
metaphyseal fixation demonstrated minimal cohort-wide changes in alignment at 1 
year postoperatively. However, a meaningful subset of patients (16%-28%) 
demonstrated clinically relevant changes in alignment, most commonly into valgus 
and decreased tibial slope. These findings warrant routine preoperative 
radiographic assessment and surveillance until skeletal maturity. Further study 
is needed to define thresholds for implant-mediated guided growth in patients 
with borderline valgus preoperatively who may be at risk of progressive 
deformity.

DOI: 10.1177/03635465261492231
PMID: 42877964
ai_summary: Transphyseal ACL reconstruction in skeletally immature patients is generally safe, though about 16-28% of patients may experience minor, clinically relevant changes in limb alignment that warrant monitoring.

title: Clinical outcomes of primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with concomitant lateral meniscal posterior root tear repair versus isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Ade-Conde M, Duru DO, Skaik K, Macciacchera M, Bouchard MD, Vincent AD, Daud A, Matache BA, Abouali J
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 12;21:101222. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101222. Online
ahead  of print.

Clinical outcomes of primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with 
concomitant lateral meniscal posterior root tear repair versus isolated anterior 
cruciate ligament reconstruction: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Ade-Conde M(1), Duru DO(2), Skaik K(3), Macciacchera M(4), Bouchard MD(5), 
Vincent AD(6), Daud A(6), Matache BA(4), Abouali J(6).



INTRODUCTION: Lateral meniscal posterior root tears (LMPRTs) commonly occur with 
anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, but clinical outcomes after 
concomitant repair remain unclear.
AIM: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared postoperative outcomes 
after ACL reconstruction (ACLR) with concomitant LMPRT repair versus isolated 
ACLR with an intact lateral meniscus and summarized available evidence comparing 
repair with nonrepair.
EVIDENCE REVIEW: MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to 
May 23, 2026. Comparative studies evaluating primary ACLR with concomitant LMPRT 
repair versus isolated ACLR with an intact lateral meniscus or untreated LMPRT 
with at least 1-year follow-up were included. The methodological quality of all 
included studies was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized 
Studies (MINORS). Meta-analyses calculated pooled mean differences (MDs) with 
95% confidence intervals (CIs) for patient-reported outcomes and objective 
stability using random-effects models. Outcomes not suitable for quantitative 
synthesis were summarized descriptively.
FINDINGS: Nine retrospective comparative studies comprising 910 knees (340 ACLR 
with LMPRT repair and 570 comparators) were included. Seven studies used 
isolated ACLR with an intact lateral meniscus as the comparator, while two 
directly compared LMPRT repair with untreated LMPRTs. Meta-analysis demonstrated 
no statistically significant between-group differences in postoperative 
International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores (MD, -0.43; 95% CI, 
-2.78 to 1.93; p = 0.72; I2 = 15%), Lysholm (MD, 0.82; 95% CI, -1.25 to 2.89; p 
= 0.44; I2 = 42%), Tegner (MD, -0.09; 95% CI, -0.43 to 0.24; p = 0.59; I2 = 
42%), or arthrometer-measured anterior tibial translation (MD, 0.23 mm; 95% CI, 
-0.04 to 0.51; p = 0.09; I2 = 73%) between ACLR with LMPRT repair and isolated 
ACLR with an intact lateral meniscus. Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome 
Score analyses showed no statistically significant differences across five 
subscales (all p ≥ 0.424), with moderate-to-high heterogeneity (I2 = 63%-84%). 
The two studies comparing repair versus untreated LMPRTs reported no 
statistically significant differences in postoperative IKDC or Lysholm scores at 
2 years (all p > 0.05). Healing according to study-specific criteria was 
observed in 89 of 110 repairs (81%).
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: ACLR with concomitant LMPRT repair showed favorable 
short-term outcomes. Comparisons with isolated ACLR with an intact lateral 
meniscus do not establish benefit over no repair, and direct evidence comparing 
repair with no repair remains limited. Future studies should determine whether 
repair technique influences outcomes and whether repair improves long-term 
chondral and radiographic outcomes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, systematic review.
PROSPERO ID: CRD420261412322.

title: Proximal fibular osteotomy for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis: clinical effectiveness and biomechanical rationale: a systematic review.
authors: Edmonds CJ, Duru D, Olamona VB, Soni D, McDonnell SM, Radhamony N
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Oct 15;63:104653. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104653. Online ahead of 
print.

Proximal fibular osteotomy for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis: clinical 
effectiveness and biomechanical rationale: a systematic review.

Edmonds CJ(1), Duru D(2), Olamona VB(2), Soni D(2), McDonnell SM(3), Radhamony 
N(3).



BACKGROUND: Proximal fibular osteotomy (PFO) has emerged as a joint-preserving 
procedure for medial compartment knee osteoarthritis (KOA). This review 
evaluated clinical effectiveness, radiographic outcomes, safety profile and 
biomechanical rationale of PFO.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and 
registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261386493). MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, 
Cochrane Library and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) were 
searched from inception to May 2026. Clinical studies evaluating PFO for medial 
compartment KOA and biomechanical, cadaveric and anatomical studies 
investigating its mechanism were included. Risk of bias was assessed using 
Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Owing to heterogeneity, 
findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Forty-five studies included 38 clinical and seven 
biomechanical/anatomical studies, representing 2,855 knees. Most reported 
improvements in pain, function and PROMs. Radiographic findings demonstrated 
modest correction and increased medial joint space width, although symptomatic 
improvement often exceeded radiographic correction. Operative time and hospital 
stay were generally short, blood loss was low, and early mobilisation was 
common. Transient common peroneal nerve dysfunction was a frequently reported 
complication; permanent neurological injury was documented, while the incidence 
of serious complications remains uncertain because of inconsistent reporting. 
Biomechanical studies demonstrated reduced medial compartment loading with 
redistribution of forces towards the lateral compartment.
CONCLUSION: Current evidence suggests PFO is associated with symptomatic 
improvement with rapid postoperative recovery, while biomechanical findings 
support a load-modifying rather than deformity-correcting mechanism. However, 
confidence in clinical effectiveness and safety is limited by predominantly 
observational evidence, heterogeneous designs and limited long-term comparative 
data.

DOI: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104653

title: Preoperative coronal phenotype is associated with the initial balance state but only weakly with final balance in robot-assisted TKA.
authors: Morita Y, Mylonakis N, Shin J, El-Hassan M, Shichman I, Kenanidis E, Tsiridis E, Sculco PK
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 13. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70648.
Online  ahead of print.

Preoperative coronal phenotype is associated with the initial balance state but 
only weakly with final balance in robot-assisted TKA.

Morita Y(1), Mylonakis N(2)(3), Shin J(1), El-Hassan M(1), Shichman I(1), 
Kenanidis E(2)(3), Tsiridis E(2)(3), Sculco PK(1).



PURPOSE: To determine how preoperative coronal phenotype and structural 
remodelling relate to initial and final intraoperative balance in robot-assisted 
total knee arthroplasty.
METHODS: Initial analyses included 429 knees; final/change analyses included 
389. Preoperative phenotype was characterised by hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), 
arithmetic HKA (aHKA), functional knee phenotype (FKP), and categorical 
aHKA-joint-line obliquity (JLO) components. Structural factors included medial 
and lateral osteophyte burden and coronal tibiofemoral subluxation. Medial and 
lateral gaps and coronal laxity ranges were recorded in extension and flexion 
before and after balancing. Signed mediolateral gap difference was defined as 
lateral minus medial, and change as final minus initial. Initial extension 
signed gap difference was the primary outcome; corresponding initial flexion, 
final, and change outcomes were secondary. Compartment-specific gaps, laxity 
ranges, and varus-valgus analyses were exploratory. Multivariable linear 
regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, with patient-level 
cluster-robust standard errors and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate 
correction.
RESULTS: The FKP model incorporating all structural factors yielded adjusted R2 
values of 0.201 for the primary outcome and 0.125 for initial flexion, leaving 
approximately 80% of primary-outcome variability unexplained. In the overall 
cohort, the maximum adjusted R2 across final outcomes was 0.064. For extension 
and flexion changes, FKP alone and HKA alone yielded adjusted R2 values of 0.234 
and 0.122, respectively. In exploratory comparisons, valgus knees had greater 
initial extension and flexion signed gap differences than varus knees (adjusted 
mean differences, 3.10 mm [95% confidence interval, 2.39-3.81] and 2.98 mm 
[2.23-3.74], respectively; both false discovery rate-adjusted p values 
were < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative coronal phenotype and structural remodelling explained 
only modest variability in the initial intraoperative balance state and changes 
between assessments, and little variability in final balance, particularly in 
flexion. These findings support direct intraoperative assessment.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

© 2026 European Society of Sports Traumatology, Knee Surgery and Arthroscopy.

DOI: 10.1002/ksa.70648
PMID: 42868008
ai_summary: Preoperative knee alignment and structure only weakly predict the final balance achieved during robot-assisted knee replacement, emphasizing the need for direct, real-time assessment during surgery.

title: High-Grade Percutaneous Medial Collateral Ligament Pie-Crusting Is Not Associated With Clinically Meaningful Valgus Instability.
authors: Nishioka T, Thamrongskulsiri N, Casanova F, Ackermann J, Morgan JT, Moews LD, Vega TF, Spaan J, Chahla J
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Oct 12:3635465261492229. doi: 10.1177/03635465261492229.
 Online ahead of print.

High-Grade Percutaneous Medial Collateral Ligament Pie-Crusting Is Not 
Associated With Clinically Meaningful Valgus Instability.

Nishioka T(1), Thamrongskulsiri N(2), Casanova F(1), Ackermann J(1), Morgan 
JT(1), Moews LD(1), Vega TF(1), Spaan J(1), Chahla J(1).



BACKGROUND: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) pie-crusting is used during medial 
meniscal surgery to improve visualization and reduce the risk of chondral 
injuries. However, some surgeons extend the release site beyond routine 
incremental perforation, and the effect of this more extensive release on 
postoperative medial laxity remains unclear.
PURPOSE: To determine whether high-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting during 
medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT) repair results in clinically 
meaningful valgus instability postoperatively as assessed by valgus stress 
radiography.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of patients who underwent isolated 
MMPRT repair with high-grade MCL pie-crusting and no prior knee ligament 
surgery. High-grade pie-crusting was defined intraoperatively by an audible and 
palpable release and a substantial medial compartment opening (≥6 mm) under 
arthroscopic visualization. Postoperative bilateral valgus stress radiographs 
were obtained at a mean of 5.9 ± 2.0 months with the knee positioned at 20° of 
flexion. Gapping was measured in millimeters, and the side-to-side difference 
was calculated using the contralateral knee as an internal control. An a priori 
power analysis based on a 3.2-mm threshold for clinically meaningful 
medial-sided laxity demonstrated a required sample size of 15 patients. The 
side-to-side difference in medial compartment gapping was analyzed using the 
1-sample t test compared with the 3.2-mm threshold.
RESULTS: A total of 21 patients met inclusion criteria. The mean medial 
compartment gapping was 7.84 ± 1.65 mm in the operative knee and 6.62 ± 1.37 mm 
in the contralateral knee. The mean side-to-side difference was 1.21 ± 1.07 mm 
(95% CI, 0.73-1.70 mm). The observed difference was significantly less than the 
3.2-mm threshold associated with clinically meaningful medial-sided instability 
(P < .001).
CONCLUSION: High-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting advanced to a defined 
intraoperative endpoint during MMPRT repair resulted in small increases in 
medial compartment gapping that remained below biomechanically defined 
instability thresholds. These preliminary findings suggest that high-grade MCL 
pie-crusting improves visualization and instrumentation without being associated 
with clinically meaningful valgus laxity postoperatively.

DOI: 10.1177/03635465261492229
PMID: 42865127
ai_summary: High-grade pie-crusting of the MCL during meniscus repair provides better surgical access without causing clinically significant knee instability.

title: Temporal distribution of recorded indications for first revision total knee arthroplasty: a multicenter Chilean cohort of 150 patients.
authors: Villanueva JI, Duque WG, Lorca MH, Acurio PE, Durruty EP, Maldonado VA, Abarca AT, Díaz Del Valle C, Manriquez HH, Rodriguez RC, Poblete DF
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 15;21:101223. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101223. Online
ahead  of print.

Temporal distribution of recorded indications for first revision total knee 
arthroplasty: a multicenter Chilean cohort of 150 patients.

Villanueva JI(1), Duque WG(2), Lorca MH(3), Acurio PE(4), Durruty EP(3), 
Maldonado VA(5), Abarca AT(4), Díaz Del Valle C(4), Manriquez HH(4), Rodriguez 
RC(3), Poblete DF(3).



INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Recorded indications for first revision total knee 
arthroplasty (TKA) may vary with time after the primary procedure. This study 
compared their distribution among early and late first revisions in a 
multicenter Chilean cohort.
METHODS: This retrospective nonconsecutive cohort included 150 unique patients 
who underwent first revision TKA at five Chilean centers between 2018 and 2026. 
Revisions were classified as early (<24 months) or late (≥24 months). Indication 
distributions were compared using categorical tests, including a fixed-margin 
Monte Carlo procedure for sparse cells. Logistic regression was adjusted for age 
and sex. Sensitivity analyses incorporated revision year and center and modeled 
time continuously, including assessment of nonlinearity.
RESULTS: The mean age was 70.1 ± 9.5 years, and 97 patients (64.7%) were women. 
Fifty-three revisions (35.3%) were early, and 97 (64.7%) were late. The 
indication distribution differed by timing (Monte Carlo p = 0.0003; Cramér's V = 
0.41). Infection was the most frequent early indication (18/53, 34.0%), whereas 
aseptic loosening accounted for more than half of late revisions (52/97, 53.6%). 
After adjustment for age and sex, late revision was associated with higher odds 
that aseptic loosening was the recorded indication (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 
6.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.80-16.00; p < 0.001). Early revision was 
associated with higher odds that infection was the recorded indication (adjusted 
OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.40-7.34; p = 0.006). Estimates were similar after accounting 
for revision year and center and when time was analyzed continuously.
CONCLUSION: Among the included first revisions, infection was the most frequent 
recorded indication before 24 months, whereas aseptic loosening was the most 
frequent indication thereafter. These within-cohort associations remain subject 
to selection bias, diagnostic misclassification, and residual confounding and do 
not estimate cause-specific revision risk after primary TKA.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Risk of Overdose and Adverse Events With Concomitant Opioids and Gabapentinoid Use After Total Joint Arthroplasty.
authors: Domingo PT, Berger GK, Gray P, Chaput R, Navarro R, Singh A
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 15;34(20):e2948-e2956. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01651. Epub 2026 May 27.

Risk of Overdose and Adverse Events With Concomitant Opioids and Gabapentinoid 
Use After Total Joint Arthroplasty.

Domingo PT(1), Berger GK, Gray P, Chaput R, Navarro R, Singh A.



PURPOSE: We evaluated the safety outcomes of opioids alone versus opioids plus 
low-dose gabapentinoids in patients naïve to both opioids and gabapentinoids, 
after total joint arthroplasty (TJA) of the knee, hip, or shoulder.
METHODS: This was a multicenter, population-based, retrospective cohort study 
based in a large, integrated health system. It included opioid-naïve and 
gabapentinoid-naïve patients who underwent TJA between 2018 and 2024. Patients 
were categorized into two groups: those dispensed opioids and low-dose 
gabapentinoids or those dispensed opioids alone postoperatively. The primary 
outcome was opioid-related overdose events. The secondary outcome was adverse 
events, including falls, fractures, neurologic/cognitive changes, sedation, and 
delirium.
RESULTS: In total, 36,351 consecutive patients comprised the study cohort, 
including 29,009 (79.8%) in the opioids-alone group and 7,342 (20.2%) in the 
opioids plus gabapentinoids group. In total, there were 19 (0.05% total cohort) 
opioid-related overdose events. Fourteen of these (0.05%) were in the 
opioids-alone group, and five (0.07%) were in the opioids plus gabapentinoids 
group ( P = 0.3). In addition, 233 patients (0.6%) experienced emergency 
department or hospital admission due to an adverse event, including 200 patients 
(0.69%) in the opioids-alone group and 33 patients (0.45%) in the opioids plus 
gabapentinoids group. No statistically significant difference in adverse event 
risk was identified between groups.
CONCLUSION: Concurrent prescriptions for opioids and low-dose gabapentinoids 
after TJA were not associated with a statistically significant difference in 
risk of emergency department or hospital readmission due to opioid-related 
overdose or adverse events compared with opioids alone. However, the rarity of 
overdose events limits statistical power, and these findings should be 
interpreted cautiously.

title: Greater three-dimensional cam burden and superolateral location are associated with end-stage hip osteoarthritis: A retrospective comparative study.
authors: Igrek S, Yigit O, Canbaz SB, Yilmaz H, Ozgur EG, Eceviz E, Kocaoglu B
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 13. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70646.
Online  ahead of print.

Greater three-dimensional cam burden and superolateral location are associated 
with end-stage hip osteoarthritis: A retrospective comparative study.

Igrek S(1), Yigit O(2), Canbaz SB(2), Yilmaz H(2), Ozgur EG(3), Eceviz E(2), 
Kocaoglu B(4).



PURPOSE: Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a recognised structural 
contributor to primary hip osteoarthritis (OA), yet many cam-positive hips do 
not progress to radiographic joint failure. This study aimed to compare 
three-dimensional cam morphology and lesion location between cam-positive hips 
with end-stage primary osteoarthritis and cam-positive, non-arthritic hips in an 
elderly fracture cohort.
METHODS: Hospital records and imaging archives from January 2020 to January 2026 
were retrospectively reviewed at a single centre. The OA group comprised 
patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty for primary OA, and the fracture 
group comprised patients aged ≥ 65 years treated for intertrochanteric or 
subtrochanteric femoral fractures without radiographic OA. Cam morphology was 
characterised using radial CT-based alpha angle, three-dimensional cam volume, 
cam/head volume ratio, and clock-face-based lesion location. Group comparisons, 
receiver operating characteristic analyses, correlation testing, and 
multivariable logistic regression were performed.
RESULTS: A total of 438 cam-positive hips were included (126 OA and 312 
fracture). OA hips demonstrated higher alpha angles (72.44° ± 5.94° vs. 
62.45° ± 5.07°), larger cam volumes (5274.77 ± 1353.26 mm3 vs. 
3215.20 ± 1524.84 mm3), higher cam/head ratios (8.61% ± 2.02% vs. 
6.35% ± 1.97%), and more superolateral lesions (52.4% vs. 36.2% anterior in the 
fracture group) (all p < 0.001). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic 
analyses identified cohort-specific discriminatory values of 66° for alpha angle 
(AUC, 0.884), 4421 mm3 for cam volume (AUC, 0.839), and 6.4% for the cam-to-head 
volume ratio (AUC, 0.791). In multivariable analyses using continuous morphology 
measures, higher alpha angle, greater cam volume, higher cam-to-head volume 
ratio, and superolateral lesion location were associated with end-stage OA-group 
membership.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with non-arthritic cam-positive hips in an elderly 
fracture cohort, end-stage primary OA hips had greater three-dimensional cam 
burden, with lesions more often located superolaterally. These retrospective 
associations do not establish longitudinal progression, causality, or individual 
prognosis.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective comparative study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, study of a non-consecutive patients, study of 
diagnostic test.

title: Mid-term clinical outcomes of one and two patient-specific mini-implants for focal (osteo-)chondral lesions of the distal femur.
authors: Rüter ML, Kösters C, den Toom DA
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Oct 11:101234. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101234. Online ahead
of  print.

Mid-term clinical outcomes of one and two patient-specific mini-implants for 
focal (osteo-)chondral lesions of the distal femur.

Rüter ML(1), Kösters C(2), den Toom DA(2).



OBJECTIVES: Patient-specific mini-metal implants may represent a treatment 
option for middle-aged patients with focal (osteo-)chondral lesions of the 
distal femur when biological repair has failed or when other individual risk 
factors make biological repair unlikely to succeed. Both single-implant 
approaches for one and dual-implant approaches for two separate lesions in the 
same knee were investigated. This study evaluates the clinical performance of 
these implants for one or two lesions in one knee.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center study was conducted using 
prospectively collected data of consecutive patients treated with one or two 
implants (Episealer® Implant, Episurf, Stockholm, Sweden) with a mean follow-up 
of 38 months. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Visual 
Analogue Scale (VAS) for pain, adverse events, and conversions to 
unicompartmental or total knee arthroplasty were assessed.
RESULTS: Statistically significant improvements in all KOOS subscales and VAS 
pain score compared to the preoperative values were observed in both groups (one 
implant n = 45; two implants n = 48; all p < 0.001). KOOS Symptoms improved from 
48.7 ± 17.9 to 74.3 ± 21.6 in the one-implant group and from 44.7 ± 15.0 to 66.0 
± 24.8 in the two-implant group. Similar improvements were observed across all 
remaining KOOS subscales. The comparison between the two groups revealed 
slightly better improvements for the one-implant group. Implant survival 
according to Kaplan-Meier analysis was 88.1% for the one-implant group (number 
at risk = 21) and 83.4% for the two-implant group (number at risk = 27) after 60 
months.
CONCLUSION: Patient-specific mini-metal implants may represent a viable 
treatment option for middle-aged patients when biological repair is not 
feasible. Within the limitations of this study, the findings suggest that this 
approach can be considered for patients with one as well as patients with two 
(osteo-)chondral lesions. An acceptable implant survival was observed, 
regardless of lesion count.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Computed Tomography Overestimates Roentgenographic Posterior Tilt in Geriatric Garden I/II Femoral Neck Fractures.
authors: Greenhill DA, Jain N, Weiss S, Lundy D
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Oct 15;34(20):e2994-e3000. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00669. Epub 2026 May 27.

Computed Tomography Overestimates Roentgenographic Posterior Tilt in Geriatric 
Garden I/II Femoral Neck Fractures.

Greenhill DA(1), Jain N, Weiss S, Lundy D.



INTRODUCTION: Current best practice is to consider primary arthroplasty for 
elderly patients with a Garden I/II femoral neck fracture (FNF) when posterior 
tilt measures greater than 20° on the lateral radiograph. Although this 
evidence-based threshold stemmed from plain radiographs, clinicians similarly 
use it using CT when available. The correspondence of posterior tilt measured on 
radiograph versus CT is unknown.
METHODS: Patients older than 65 years presenting with a Garden I/II FNF during a 
6.5-year period (January 2018 to August 2024) were retrospectively reviewed. 
Patients without concomitant radiograph and CT of the affected hip or with 
inadequate radiographs were excluded. Posterior tilt of the FNF was measured on 
lateral radiographs (PT-XR) and compared with CT (PT-CT).
RESULTS: After review of 1,244 records, a total of 100 patients averaging 82 ± 8 
years old met inclusion criteria. Twenty-nine patients underwent internal 
fixation and 71 hemiarthroplasty. On average, PT-CT was larger than PT-XR (14° 
vs. 9°; P < 0.001). Lateral radiographs identified two patients (2%) with a 
posterior tilt ≥20°, while CT identified 17 (17%). For the 15 patients in whom 
increased posterior tilt was identified only by CT, the mean difference between 
PT-XR and PT-CT was 24 ± 15°.
CONCLUSION: In patients with Garden I/II FNFs, CT often generates larger 
posterior tilt measurements than plain radiographs. Using CT, an additional 15% 
of these patients are identified as having posterior tilt ≥20°. Therefore, 
advanced imaging of Garden I/II FNFs objectively increases the number of 
fractures considered too unstable for internal fixation. However, its use as an 
indication for primary arthroplasty is not yet evidence based.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Previous bariatric surgery before knee arthroplasty: A cautious interpretation.
authors: Qu X, Sun G, Chen B
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Oct 13. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70640.
Online  ahead of print.

Previous bariatric surgery before knee arthroplasty: A cautious interpretation.

Qu X(1), Sun G(1), Chen B(1).



We read with interest the nationwide register-based study by Aljuboori et al. 
examining previous bariatric surgery (BAS) and reintervention after knee 
arthroplasty. The authors appropriately state that their findings do not 
establish a benefit of BAS or negate the influence of residual obesity. We 
highlight several interpretive constraints. Matching on body mass index (BMI) at 
arthroplasty conditions on a post-exposure variable, while restriction to 
patients who ultimately underwent arthroplasty excludes those who improved 
sufficiently to avoid surgery. The 95% confidence interval for 2-year 
reintervention supports the absence of a statistically detectable difference, 
not equivalence or non-inferiority. Two-year follow-up may miss later mechanical 
failures, and exclusion of approximately 9% of screened records, including 
patients with missing BMI, may introduce additional selection bias. 
Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists remain an important future 
perspective. Overall, the study provides useful short-term conditional 
observational evidence among selected arthroplasty recipients with comparable 
BMI, rather than an estimate of the overall causal effect of BAS before knee 
arthroplasty.

PMID: 42868003
ai_summary: This commentary cautions against drawing broad conclusions about bariatric surgery's benefit before knee replacement, noting that existing research has significant limitations in study design and follow-up duration.

title: Visual presentation, statistical reporting and methodological considerations in a meta-analysis of remnant-preserving anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Xiong Q, Wang X, Fu W
abstract:

Online  ahead of print.

Visual presentation, statistical reporting and methodological considerations in 
a meta-analysis of remnant-preserving anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Xiong Q(1), Wang X(1)(2), Fu W(1).



This Letter addresses critical methodological inconsistencies in a recent 
meta-analysis on remnant-preserving anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. 
We identify specific errors in statistical reporting and forest-plot 
visualization. A reconstructed analysis is provided to ensure accurate 
interpretation of clinical stability outcomes.
